title: A logarithmic equation
steps: Logarithms accept every real input, so no domain restriction is required.
Apply the sum rule $\ln a + \ln b = \ln(a+b)$: $\ln x + \ln(x-2) = \ln(2x-2)$.
The natural logarithm is one-to-one, so $2x - 2 = 3$.

clean_steps: Both arguments must be positive: $x > 0$ and $x - 2 > 0$, so the domain is $x > 2$.
The equation is $\ln(x(x-2)) = \ln 3$. Because $\ln$ is one-to-one, $x(x-2) = 3$.
Only $x = 3$ lies in the domain $x > 2$. The candidate $x = -1$ is excluded.

errors.original: Require both arguments to be positive: $x > 0$ and $x - 2 > 0$, so the domain is $x > 2$.
errors.corrupted: Logarithms accept every real input, so no domain restriction is required.
errors.why_wrong: $\ln t$ is defined only for positive $t$. Each argument needs its own inequality, and together they restrict the domain to $x > 2$.
errors.why_tempting: Once both logarithms are already written down, the restriction feels like bookkeeping rather than part of solving.
errors.catch_rule: Before using a logarithm identity, write the inequalities that make every argument positive, and test every candidate against them.
errors.hint: Where is a logarithm defined, and which candidates would that exclude?

errors.original: Apply the product identity $\ln a + \ln b = \ln(ab)$, so $\ln x + \ln(x-2) = \ln(x(x-2))$.
errors.corrupted: Apply the sum rule $\ln a + \ln b = \ln(a+b)$: $\ln x + \ln(x-2) = \ln(2x-2)$.
errors.why_wrong: A sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product, $\ln a + \ln b = \ln(ab)$, not the logarithm of a sum. The swapped operation changes $x(x-2) = 3$ into $2x - 2 = 3$.
errors.why_tempting: The plus sign between the logarithms is easy to copy inside as a plus, on the model of distributing the function over addition.
errors.catch_rule: When you combine logarithms, say the operation out loud: a sum of logs is the log of a product.
errors.hint: The rule used to combine the two logarithms names the right idea and the wrong operation.

meta.blurb: Solve an equation that adds two logarithms.
